212	// This avoids network calls on every push — once the branch exists locally, this is a no-op.
213	// It runs on the push hot path, so it uses the short fetch budget.
214	//
215	// A fetch failure is not fatal — the push will create the branch on the remote
216	// when it succeeds — but it is returned rather than swallowed so the caller can
217	// log it. Returning nil unconditionally meant a checkpoint remote that was
218	// unreachable, too slow, or refusing auth looked identical to one that was never
219	// contacted, and resolvePushSettings' warning could never fire.
220	//
221	// A remote that simply does not carry the branch yet (the normal state of a
222	// brand-new checkpoint repo) is not a failure and stays quiet. That case is
223	// established by probing with ls-remote first — positive evidence, matching
224	// remote.FetchCheckpointRef's absence-vs-failure contract — rather than by
225	// treating every fetch error as absence.
226	//
227	// The probe and the fetch share one deadline, so the budget the caller sees is
228	// the constant's value rather than twice it: per-call timeouts do not compose

240		// would send us to the network to fix a local problem.
241		refs := checkpoint.ResolveRefs(ctx)
